newsitem.title: FRANCE: New space race takes off in satellite factories.
newsitem.headline: New space race takes off in satellite factories.

text.p: Rising demand for communications satellites is spurring a space race between manufacturers, who are turning to mass production and curbing custom designs, company officials at the Paris airshow said.

The civilian market -- satellites, launches and ground stations -- is expected to surpass $30 billion worldwide this year, a ten-fold increase from a decade ago, with sustained growth anticipated over the next five years.
The satellites often cost more than $100 million and operators are pushing manufacturers to get them into orbit -- and making money -- faster than ever.

Heavy satellites placed in geostationary orbit continue to dominate telecommunications and the market. Constellations of lighter satellites for lower orbits will only be operational in several years' time.
Industry leader Hughes Space & Communications, with 29 percent of world orders, uses almost assembly line methods to manufacture satellites at its Los Angeles plant.

Competitors are looking at similar methods to produce spacecraft whose delicate equipment must survive the stress of rocket launches and then operate flawlessly in space for 15 years. Satellites have in the past been custom-made items, but that is no longer possible.
France's Aerospatiale , with 14 percent of the market, is slated to deliver its first new generation Spacebus 4000 satellite in late 1999.

"Our objective is to eventually manufacture Spacebus 4000 in 18 months. Currently we need 30 to 36 months," Henri Sala, director of satellite operations for Aerospatiale, told a news conference on Friday.
Sala said mass production methods at the company's plant in Cannes, France, will be the decisive factor to increase productivity and market share.

Not to be outdone is U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin , which currently holds 17 percent of the market and will be opening a new satellite production plant employing 1,200 people in Pennsylvania next month.

Mike Henshaw, president of the company's Space and Missiles division told Reuters: "Quick satellite production cycle time is what the market demands, because companies want their (satellite) transponders in orbit.
"Maybe for the military four-year satellite development time is fine. In that amount of time I will have built 36 satellites."

He added: "It's 18 months going to 12 -- it has to go to 12 because the world's competition demands it...You will never get to 12 months without common products and repeatable process. There can no longer be unique designs for every satellite, there must be some commonality," Henshaw said.
But reduced production time of satellites has had dramatic consequences for the schedules of satellite launchers.

The Arianespace company that has half of the world's launch market can launch rockets every three weeks from its pad in Kourou, French Guiana in South America. So far this year, however, only four launches have taken place, with hastily-built satellites being pulled off their manifest at the last minute.

"We are accelerating our activities this summer because we have waited for satellites and these satellites are finally, though with considerable delay, ready for launch," said Roger Solari, Arianespace's Guiana operations director.
"It's understandable that a client cannot take a risk to launch a satellite when a defect in that satellite has been detected, but for us this creates problems," he said.
